findings.explanation: Of the equal 20-month windows in Biden's term, the script picks his first (Jan 2021 to Sep 2022, 13.5%), which holds the 2022 inflation peak (12-month rate 9.1% in June 2022). His last 20 months, May 2023 to Jan 2025 (304.127 to 317.671), rose about 4.5%, less than this term's 6.1%. So 'still well above this term's rise' depends on which equal window you pick, and the verdict's own like-for-like figure (annualized 5.0% against 3.6%) is a much smaller gap than 13.5 against 6.1.
findings.suggestion: Give both ends of Biden's term: his first 20 months rose 13.5 percent, his last 20 (May 2023 to January 2025) about 4.5 percent (calc (317.671 / 304.127 - 1) * 100), against 6.1 percent since. Say this term's pace is slower than his term as a whole, not 'well above' over any equal stretch.

findings.explanation: 'Prices have risen less under this term so far, even over equal stretches' holds only for the start-of-term window. Over Biden's last 20 months the CPI rose about 4.5% (May 2023 304.127 to Jan 2025 317.671), less than this term's 6.1%. The evidence supports 'less than across his full term, at a slower annual pace' (verdict: 5.0% against 3.6%), not 'less over equal stretches' in general.
findings.suggestion: Say: 'So prices have risen more slowly this term than across Biden's term as a whole, though faster than in his last stretch, and by a smaller margin than the totals suggest; and the index cannot say how much of either rise any president caused.'
